# Fractal Units, Not Fractal Bureaucracy {#sec-fractal-units}

As a company adds business lines, it faces a familiar choice. Centralize decisions and slow the edges, or decentralize and accept duplication. The choice is false when the organization has not specified what must be shared.

ATOM uses the term **Fractal Unit** for a semi-autonomous group that can run a complete governed outcome loop. “Fractal” does not mean every unit is identical. It means the same operating grammar recurs at different scales: intent, context, decisions, execution, evidence, learning, and control.

The repeatable object is not the team diagram. It is the contract.

## The unit contract

Every unit should be able to state:

| Element | Contract |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Customer or enterprise outcome the unit exists to produce |
| Economics | Revenue, cost, margin, assets, or risk it owns and can observe |
| Inputs and outputs | What enters, what leaves, and in what form |
| Decisions | Rights held locally, shared, and at the center |
| Dependencies | Services and capacities required from others |
| Context | Sources and policies required to operate |
| Controls | Non-negotiable limits and escalation conditions |
| Evidence | Measures, traces, and review obligations |
| Learning | What the unit may change and what requires shared approval |
| Lifecycle | Conditions to grow, split, merge, or close |

A unit without outcome ownership is a project team. A unit without visible economics is a cost center pretending to be a business. A unit without bounded rights is a reporting layer.

## Invariants and local choices

Scale depends on making a few things rigid enough that everything else can adapt.

Invariants may include customer identity, financial definitions, security controls, core product interfaces, evidence requirements, and rules for allocating shared assets. Units should not invent their own meaning of active customer or contribution margin. They should not bypass access policy because the central service is slow.

Local choices include workflow, roles, experiments, tools, and decisions inside the unit's authority envelope. The center should resist standardizing them simply because one unit found a successful pattern. Reuse should follow evidence and compatible conditions, not executive preference.

## Illustrative example: two locally correct decisions

A company adds an energy-services unit beside its original equipment business. Both use the same field engineers and device platform.

The equipment unit schedules engineers to protect installation revenue. The services unit promises response times to win recurring contracts. Each choice is rational inside its own P&L. Together they oversubscribe the same asset, and both units miss commitments.

The first response is a central capacity committee. Every exception moves upward. The meeting becomes the operating system.

The better design exposes available engineering capacity as a shared service with a clear owner, reservation rules, priority classes, cost, and exception path. Each unit decides inside its allocation. The center sets the portfolio tradeoff and capacity buffer. Evidence shows demand, utilization, missed commitments, and the economic value of each use.

The units remain different. The interface becomes stable.

## Where work belongs

Place a capability inside a unit when it requires deep local context, changes frequently with the offer, and can be owned end to end. Share it when scale, scarce expertise, risk consistency, or a common asset creates real advantage. Keep it at the center when the decision sets enterprise intent, allocates capital among units, defines non-negotiable policy, or resolves a conflict the unit cannot legitimately settle.

Do not decide from ideology. Centralization has a latency cost; decentralization has duplication and divergence costs. Make both visible.

The fractal hypothesis has a boundary. Constantly re-forming teams destroys relationships and accumulated context. Physical assets do not reallocate like cloud capacity. Regulated accountability may remain centralized even when execution does not. A stable unit with clear interfaces is often more adaptive than a fluid network that renegotiates ownership every week.

What repeats at scale is a governed outcome loop. When unit contracts are explicit, local autonomy and enterprise coherence stop being opposites.
